name: UCC27524DR
title: Dual 5 A high-speed low-side gate driver, non-inverting, inputs rated to -5 V
summary: The UCC27524 holds two separate low-side gate-drive channels, each non-inverting with its own enable, able to push and pull 5 A peaks into a MOSFET or IGBT gate from a 4.5 V to 18 V supply. Input and enable thresholds are fixed TTL/CMOS levels with about 1 V of hysteresis, independent of VDD, and the D and DGN inputs survive -5 V. Typical propagation delay is 17 ns with 1 ns matching between channels, so the two channels may be paralleled. It comes in SOIC-8 (D), HVSSOP-8 with exposed pad (DGN), 3 mm x 3 mm WSON-8 (DSD) and PDIP-8 (P).

pins.name: ENA
pins.function: Enable for channel A, active high. Low forces OUTA low whatever INA does; high or open lets channel A run. An internal pullup to VDD (200 kΩ typ) keeps it enabled when open, so the pin may float, matching the N/C pin 1 of the UCC27324.

pins.name: INA
pins.function: Non-inverting logic input of channel A. An internal pulldown to GND (120 kΩ typ) keeps OUTA low when INA is open.

pins.name: INB
pins.function: Non-inverting logic input of channel B. An internal pulldown to GND keeps OUTB low when INB is open.

pins.name: OUTB
pins.function: Gate-drive output of channel B, swinging from GND to VDD.

pins.name: VDD
pins.function: Bias supply, 4.5 V to 18 V; also the source of every output current pulse.

pins.name: OUTA
pins.function: Gate-drive output of channel A, swinging from GND to VDD.

pins.name: ENB
pins.function: Enable for channel B, active high. Low forces OUTB low whatever INB does; high or open lets channel B run. Pulled up internally so it may float, matching the N/C pin 8 of the UCC27324.

pins.name: PAD
pins.function: Exposed thermal pad on the underside. It joins no lead, but ties electrically and thermally to the die substrate, which is device ground. Soldering it to GND copper with thermal vias is recommended, for heat removal and EMI immunity.

circuits.title: Typical application, two low-side MOSFETs (Figure 8-1)
circuits.description: Each channel drives the gate of its own N-channel MOSFET through a series gate resistor; both MOSFET sources go to ground and each drain leaves the figure as a connection to the power stage. INA, INB, ENA and ENB come in from the controller as separate lines. The VDD rail V+ has one bypass capacitor to GND at the chip.

circuits.title: Driving the IGBT of a boost converter, channels paralleled (Figure 8-3)
circuits.description: Both channels act as one stronger driver: INA and INB are joined to the single controller signal, ENA and ENB are tied to the bias rail VBias so the part is always enabled, and OUTA and OUTB are joined. The combined output reaches the IGBT gate through two paths in parallel: a resistor alone, and a second resistor in series with a diode, the resistor on the driver side and the diode's cathode toward it, so turn-off can sink through both paths. The IGBT is the switch of a boost stage: Vin feeds the boost inductor, the switch node runs through the boost diode to Vout, an output capacitor holds Vout, and Vout goes to the load. CVDD decouples VBias at the driver. The IGBT has 110 nC of gate charge.

operation.text: Total VDD current is the quiescent current plus the average output current, QG × fSW, plus whatever flows in the enable pullups. With outputs static (DC high or low) the quiescent current is at its lowest with all logic running. Supply current against frequency at three VDD values, both channels switching 1.8 nF, rises linearly, which shows almost no shoot-through current inside the driver.

INA and INB use TTL/CMOS thresholds that do not move with VDD: typically 2 V rising and 1 V falling, about 1 V of hysteresis, so 3.3 V and 5 V controllers drive them directly. Input capacitance is very low. A pulldown on each input to GND holds its output low if the input is left open. The D and DGN inputs withstand -5 V. The inputs want fast edges (under 200 ns), as a PWM controller or a logic gate gives; a slowly moving input can make the output toggle repeatedly at high frequency. Where slower switching edges are wanted, a resistor from driver output to gate is recommended; it also takes some of the gate-charge loss out of the package.

ENA and ENB are active-high, one per channel, with the same VDD-independent TTL/CMOS thresholds as the inputs. Internal pullups to VDD (200 kΩ typ) enable both channels when the pins are open, so they can be left unconnected; this keeps the part pin-compatible with the UCC27323, UCC27324 and UCC27325, whose pins 1 and 8 are N/C. Enable is used, for example, to switch off synchronous-rectifier drive at light load. When the two channels are paralleled, ENA and ENB are tied and driven together.

The pullup is a P-channel and an N-channel MOSFET in parallel. The N-channel device conducts only for a short moment at each low-to-high transition, giving a burst of extra source current through the Miller plateau; its on-resistance is about 1.04 Ω. ROH is a DC figure for the P-channel device alone, so the effective pullup resistance during turn-on is much lower than ROH. The pulldown is a single N-channel MOSFET, described by ROL. Each output sources and sinks 5 A peaks and swings rail to rail with very little drop. Body diodes clamp overshoot and undershoot, and the outputs tolerate 5 A peak reverse current transients. Low drop in both states suits a gate-drive transformer driven between OUTA and OUTB with INA and INB complementary. Peak current is higher at higher VDD; 5 A is the figure at VDD = 12 V, and the driver supplies about 5 A for several hundred nanoseconds at that voltage.

Delay from input to output is 17 ns typical, and the two channels match within 1 ns typical (2 ns max). This suits synchronous rectifiers and paralleled MOSFETs driven from one PFC signal. The channels can be combined into one driver of twice the current by joining INA to INB and OUTA to OUTB. A difference in input threshold between the channels, made worse by slow input edges, can then delay one output against the other and drive shoot-through current between them. When the outputs are joined directly, drive INA and INB with edges of at least 20 V/µs and connect them right at the pins. Footprints for series gate resistors on OUTA and OUTB give the choice of 0 Ω links or resistance to limit that current.

Below the UVLO threshold the outputs are held low whatever the inputs do. The threshold is about 4 V with about 300 mV of hysteresis, which rides out supply noise and the VDD dip when switching begins. At power-up, with enable high or open, the output stays low until VDD reaches the threshold, then follows the input, its amplitude rising with VDD to the final level. Operation below 5 V suits GaN switches. When operating near 4.5 V, the supply ripple must stay below the hysteresis VDD_H, or the part shuts down; at power-down it runs until VDD falls below VOFF, and at start-up it waits for VON.

VDD runs from 4.5 V, set by UVLO, to 18 V, which leaves 2 V of margin under the 20 V absolute maximum for transients. Every output source pulse is drawn through VDD, so low-ESR ceramic surface-mount bypass capacitors go between VDD and GND right at the chip: a 100 nF (0.1 µF) capacitor nearest the pins, and a larger low-ESR capacitor of about 1 µF to a few µF in parallel beside it.

Package dissipation depends on the gate charge of the switch at the drive voltage (VGS is close to VDD because VOH drop is small), the switching frequency and any external gate resistance. Quiescent current and shoot-through are small enough to neglect. Half of PG is lost charging the gate and half discharging it.

Put the driver close to the power device so the output-to-gate traces are short. Place the VDD-to-GND bypass capacitors right beside the driver on short traces; use SMD resistors and capacitors for low inductance. Keep the turn-on and turn-off loops (driver, power MOSFET, bypass capacitor) as small as possible, since high di/dt in them induces transients at OUT and at the gate. Run source and return traces side by side for flux cancellation. Keep power traces away from signal traces. Use star grounding: driver GND, the MOSFET source and the controller ground meet at one point over short, wide paths. A ground plane gives shielding against fast OUT edges coupling into the inputs; it must carry no loop current and joins the star point by one trace; it also helps spread heat. Replacing a UCC2732x or UCC2742x needs care: this part is stronger (5 A against 4 A peak) and faster (17 ns/17 ns against 25 ns/35 ns delays).

The DGN (HVSSOP-8) package has an exposed pad under the body that conducts heat out through the board, giving much better heat-sinking than the D package. The board needs thermal lands and thermal vias under it. The pad is joined to the substrate, which is device ground, and to no lead; connect it to GND for EMI immunity. The DSD pad must be soldered for thermal and mechanical performance.

Input-to-output delay tD1 runs from the input crossing VINx_H to the output reaching 10 %; tD2 from the input crossing VINx_L to the output falling to 90 %, with enable high. Enable delay tD3 runs from enable crossing VENx_H to the output reaching 10 %; tD4 from enable crossing VENx_L to the output falling to 90 %, with the input high.
